lesson.title: Nicht & Kein
lesson.subtitle: not and nicht are the same 'no-thing' — and each has its own job

hook.title: No-Thing, Twice
hook.content: English built not from nāwiht — 'no thing'. German built nicht from ni wiht — 'never a creature'. Same recipe, same ancient word for 'being' (English kept it in the archaic wight), and German even pronounces the old gh: nicht's ch is the gh of naught, still sounding after a thousand years of English silence. But German splits the job: nouns are negated with kein (not one), verbs and adjectives with nicht. English has one not for everything; German has a not for things and a not for actions.

footnotes.title: The gh You Can Finally Hear
footnotes.content: not ← nāwiht and nicht ← ni wiht both contained the guttural gh. English silenced it; German kept it as ch. When you say nicht, you are pronouncing the h that English spelling still writes in 'nought' but never sounds.

pattern.title: kein for Nouns, nicht for Verbs
pattern.content:
Negating a noun? Use kein, declined exactly like ein: Ich habe kein Haus (I have no house), keine Zeit (no time), keinen Kaffee (not a coffee — the Him-Case again!). Negating a verb or adjective? Use nicht: Ich kann nicht kommen (I cannot come), Das ist nicht gut (that is not good). Placement: nicht usually lands at the end of simple clauses, right where the action dies. Ich weiß es nicht — I know it not: three words, one of them the twin of wise (weiß), one the twin of it (es).

One Denglisch ladder, read it the German way first: Ich will nicht gehen → I want not to go → I don't want to go. The odd middle line is the lesson: nicht sits right before the bare infinitive, exactly where English 'not' sat before want and will merged and English shipped its 'not' forward.
pattern.trap_note: Your mind will offer: “not is one word, one place.” German has two negations doing two jobs — nicht negates verbs and adjectives, kein negates a *noun* and then declines like ein. If you reach for nicht in front of a noun, that is the slip: you want kein.
pattern.linguist_note: kein ← nekein ← ni + ein ('not one') is the exact parallel of English none ← 'not one'. The languages negated possession with the same arithmetic — and German never let the word shrink.

exercises.explanation: Nouns take kein (declined like ein): keine Zeit. nicht is for verbs and adjectives.

exercises.prompt: Match each negated sentence with its English meaning:
exercises.target_answer: Ich kann nicht kommen, Ich habe kein Haus, Das ist nicht gut, Wir haben keine Zeit, nicht laut — leise, Das Getränk ist nicht billig, keine Insel, kein Nebel heute
exercises.meaning: I cannot come, I have no house, that is not good, we have no time, not loud — quiet, the drink is not cheap, no island, no fog today
exercises.explanation: Verbs and adjectives take nicht; noun phrases take kein, declined like ein: die Insel → keine Insel, der Nebel → kein Nebel. Two negations, two jobs.

exercises.prompt: Which English is built the German way?
exercises.explanation: kein negates the noun — the German says, word for word, 'I want no cup.' English rebuilt the sentence with don't; German kept the no-thing word sitting right where the cup is.

exercises.prompt: Which of these are honest English for Ich will nicht gehen?
renderings: I do not want to go
exercises.target_answer: I don't want to go, I do not want to go
exercises.explanation: The same thought, several honest English shapes — and none of them is the word-for-word one. German says it the literal way ('I want not to go') and English does not. That asymmetry is the whole lesson of topic 12, and it is why you translate thoughts, never words.
exercises.affirmation: You passed on the literal rendering and kept the natural ones — that is thought-translation, not word-matching.

exercises.idea: the question was about it — the thing, the plan, whatever it was — and your honest answer: you do not know it
cues: Know is wissen → ich weiß (the wise twin, sharp ß and all)
nicht kills the verb and lands where the action dies: at the very end

vocab_hints.note: es ↔ it — the same ancient pronoun. In speech you might hear it cling to the verb: hat's (hat es), ist's (ist es) — recognize them, no pressure to use them.
from wissen — the same root as wise; the ß is the sharp S of the T→SS shift

exercises.explanation: nicht lands at the end where the action dies: 'Ich weiß es nicht' — I know it not.

diagnosis.slip: nicht drifted to the English seat
diagnosis.cue: English merged want/will and shipped its 'not' forward; German kept the ancient seat — nicht goes where the action dies, at the end: Ich weiß es nicht.

summary.outcome: Choose between kein and nicht correctly and place nicht at the clause end.
summary.takeaway: Nouns take kein ('not one'), verbs and adjectives take nicht ('no-thing') — the two negations English merged into one not.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the kein vs nicht choice gym — twenty prompts naming which no-thing kills the noun and which kills the verb.

twist.prompt: Now kill the verb: I can come tomorrow becomes I cannot come tomorrow. (nicht's seat: right before the bare infinitive.)
twist.explanation: nicht negates what follows it, so it sits right before the bare infinitive — inside the bracket, after morgen. Word for word: 'I can tomorrow not come.'

nicht.etymology_derivation: OHG niowiht: 'never a creature/thing' — the same no-thing story as English not ← nāwiht, kin to archaic wight 'being'. The gh of naught survives as German ch. [wiktionary]

kein.etymology_derivation: Back-formation of nekein 'not any' (ni + ein, 'not one') — built right on ein, exactly like English none ← 'not one'. [wiktionary]

können.context_translation: I can come / I am able to come.
können.etymology_derivation: Originally meant "to know/understand". Preserved in English "can", "cunning" (knowing how), "uncanny", and "beyond my ken" (beyond my knowledge).

zeit.etymology_derivation: t → z [ts] (cognate with English "tide", as in Yuletide or time and tide).

haus.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hūsą — an exact twin of English house, down to the diphthong. [wiktionary]

kurz.etymology_derivation: From Latin curtus — the same Latin word as English curt; NOT related to short. [wiktionary]

laut.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *hlūd; only Old Saxon hlūd compared — the loud link is not on the page. [wiktionary]

leise.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *līs(ī) 'low, soft'; no cognates named — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

billig.etymology_derivation: Old High German billīh 'appropriate', kin to Bild/bilden; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

insel.context_translation: The island lies in the south.
insel.etymology_derivation: From Old High German isila, borrowed from Latin insula. English isle and insular come from the same Latin word. [wiktionary]

nebel.context_phrase: Im Herbst gibt es oft Nebel.
nebel.context_translation: In autumn there is often fog.
nebel.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *nebulaz, from PIE *nébʰos — inherited Germanic, PIE-kin to English nebula. [wiktionary]

baum.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *baumaz — English beam is the cognate; a beam was originally a tree. [wiktionary]

getränk.etymology_derivation: Getränk — a collective built on the old word Trank (drink), the same root as trinken; English drink shows the old d where German shifted it to t. [wiktionary]

tasse.etymology_derivation: Via Middle French tasse from Arabic tas, meaning bowl, itself from Middle Persian tasht; English keeps the same word in the dialectal tass, while standard English uses cup. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
